doc.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Beginnings of the Elvin Jones Jazz Machine
summary: He says the Jazz Machine began with Garrison and Farrell, with members changing over the years.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: So the Elvin Jones Jazz Machine has been stem rolling for several decades. Ken Kimery and I first saw that group in 1980 in Mannheim, Germany. At that time you had Andrew White, Ari Brown, Ryo? Was he playing guitar?
Ryo Kawasaki? No. It was Marvin Horn, I think he was playing guitar.
Tell us a little bit about the beginning of the Elvin Jones Jazz Machine, and if you had a particular vision for that group.
I didn’t have any particular vision for that group because we started, the Jazz Machine with Jimmy Garrison and Joe Farrell (Laughs).
(Laughs) Okay, it just didn’t have that name then?
But the idea and the concept was in place.

Yeah you just add or subtract from that. But it’s sort of if it’s meant to be, it will be. That means, that’s how much effort you’re going to put into it. If you’re wholehearted, if you’re ready to die for it, that’s what you’re meant to do. You certainly have to have that kind of courage.
Who have been some of the members of the Jazz Machine that you particularly have a fond memory of and anything, if you’d like to share that with us?

I don’t know anybody that I can pick one over the other. There’s been a lot of people, we’ve enjoyed each other’s company for many years on different occasions. We experienced things together. I try and tell guys, “When we are on the road you have to look out for your colleague. You keep your eye on him; he’ll keep his eye on you.” That means you learn how to love each other, and take care of each other, and be responsible in certain ways. That’s always part of the lesson. (Laughs)
